La prima notte di quiete (1972) is a quiet, haunting story about a man who is simply worn out by life.

Directed by Valerio Zurlini, the film shows a very different side of Rimini. There are no sunny beaches or glamorous nights. Instead, we see grey winter skies, empty streets, and buildings that seem to be slowly falling apart. The setting feels cold and tired — just like the main character.

At the center of the story is Daniele Dominici, played by Alain Delon in one of his most vulnerable performances. Daniele is a teacher who arrives in town wearing a worn camel-hair coat, looking as if he hasn’t slept in days. He isn’t starting over. He’s drifting. Beneath his calm surface is disappointment, regret, and a quiet despair he can’t shake.

When he becomes involved with his student Vanina, their relationship doesn’t feel like a typical love story. It feels more like two lonely people recognizing the same sadness in each other. They aren’t chasing happiness — they’re searching for relief.

The film moves with steady melancholy, never offering easy hope. Its title, “The First Night of Quiet,” hints at something unsettling: for some people, peace may not come through love or rest, but only through the stillness of death.

With its somber music and stark winter imagery, the film becomes a poetic reflection on exhaustion, longing, and the strange beauty that can exist inside sadness.
